clue.text: One holding groceries and dancing lively dance for Spooner

indicators.note: for here means in place of, so the opening sound of the other word takes over this word's opening

parts.note: bopping is dancing to pop music

indicators.note: Spooner names Dr Spooner, whose slip was trading the opening sounds of two words, so this word takes the other's opening

parts.note: the shag is a lively swing dance from the 1930s

explanation.surface: A shopper with groceries dances a lively dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for Spooner' asks for a Spoonerism: BOPPING (dancing) and SHAG (a lively dance) trade their opening sounds, B and SH, giving SHOPPING and BAG. The shag is an American swing dance; in Britain the word is also coarse slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopping bag is a carrier used to hold and carry home bought food and goods.

clue.text: Silverware half-heartedly put on gold support

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part sits on top of the second

parts.note: SPOONS losing one of its two central Os
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Silver cutlery set, rather listlessly, on a golden stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' looks like a noun at the end of the surface, but it works as the verb: to sponsor someone is to back them.
explanation.definitionFit: To sponsor someone is to support them, often with money.

clue.text: Now and again, go wrong as trek is not simple

indicators.note: only now and then, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the even letters: gO wRoNg As TrEk

explanation.surface: A hike that sometimes goes astray proves complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go wrong' tempts you to look for an anagram indicator; here it is simply part of the fodder whose every second letter is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ornate is elaborate, the opposite of simple.

clue.text: Parking supplementing new train station

parts.note: P is the parking sign
supplementing is adding to
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Extra car parking is added at a newly opened railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington is a main-line railway terminus in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddington is one of London's big railway stations.

clue.text: Question ultimately raised in public denial

indicators.note: ultimately picks the final letter of question

parts.note: its last letter is used

indicators.note: raised in says that letter is lifted out of the word for public, to go to the top of this down entry

parts.note: open means public, available to all

explanation.surface: A public figure is asked a question and gives an emphatic no.
explanation.walkthrough: OPEN (public) ends in N, the last letter of 'Question'; 'raised in' lifts that N from the bottom of OPEN to the top of this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nope is an informal, emphatic way of saying no, so it is a flat refusal or denial.

clue.text: Prominence of Cyrano de Bergerac with involvement of one VIP

indicators.note: one is involved in, so placed inside, the other

parts.note: Cyrano is famous for his very large nose
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Cyrano's famous nose makes him stand out as a very important person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prominence' reads as fame, but here it is literally the part that sticks out: Cyrano's big nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A big noise is slang for an important person, a VIP.

clue.text: Fellow eats last of Cheddar before Swiss cheese

indicators.note: the first part swallows the second
the final letter of 'Cheddar'

parts.note: a guy is a fellow
last letter of CheddaR
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A man finishes the Cheddar before moving on to a Swiss cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like a time link in the surface, but it supplies ERE, the old poetic word for before.
explanation.definitionFit: Gruyère is a hard cheese from Switzerland.

clue.text: Brother on vacation had tanned

indicators.note: vacated, emptied of its middle, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: BROTHER emptied
to have something is to own it

explanation.surface: A brother comes back from holiday with a suntan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' tempts you to think of holidays and suntans, but it tells you to empty BROTHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Browned and tanned both describe skin darkened by the sun.

clue.text: Life begins at forty: resolved to leave for sea organised appropriately

indicators.note: resolved here means broken down and re-formed, so the whole phrase's letters are rearranged
to leave says the named letters must go out of the rearranged phrase
organised means put in order, so the letters of for sea may come out of the phrase in any arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A man decides at forty that life begins, and resolves to go to sea in an orderly way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' rearranges LIFE BEGINS AT FORTY, and 'to leave' takes out the letters of FOR SEA ('organised', in any order), leaving eleven letters that spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Befittingly means in a way that is suitable or proper, a close synonym of appropriately.

clue.text: Dick hurt back getting edible tubers

parts.note: a dick is slang for a detective, so PI, a private investigator

indicators.note: back means going backwards, so the word for hurt is read in reverse

parts.note: stung means hurt

explanation.surface: A man called Dick hurts his back digging up edible roots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' looks like a man's name, but it is slang for a detective, PI. 'back' reverses STUNG (hurt) to GNUTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pignuts are the small edible underground tubers of the earthnut plant, foraged in British woods.

clue.text: What salesperson at marina might do displays theatricality

definitions.text: What salesperson at marina might do
definitions.meaning: a cryptic hint: a boat dealer shows a customer round a vessel, split into three words

explanation.surface: A boat salesman puts on quite a show for his customers.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a cryptic hint: a boat dealer might SHOW a MAN a SHIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a flair for performance and display is theatricality, while the split reading gives the literal sales pitch.

clue.text: Break down about this novel's bleak end, perhaps

definitions.note: a bleak is a small river fish, so its end is an example of the answer

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for break down goes round the jumbled letters

parts.note: to fail is to break down

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of this take a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A reader despairs over a novel with a bleak ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bleak' reads as gloomy, but it is a small freshwater fish, so its end is its tail, and 'perhaps' marks the definition as an example. 'novel' and 'about' sit naturally in a book review.
explanation.definitionFit: The bleak is a small silvery freshwater fish, so the tail at its rear is an example of the answer.

clue.text: Jacket having bad smell worn by character cycling

indicators.note: worn by means wrapped around, so the smell's letters enclose the other piece

parts.note: BO is body odour, a bad smell

indicators.note: cycling means going round, so the opening letter of the word moves to the end

parts.note: a role is a character played by an actor

explanation.surface: A cyclist's jacket smells bad after riding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' looks like riding a bike, but it means moving a letter round from the front of the word to the back; BO is the standard abbreviation for body odour.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolero is a short open jacket ending above the waist, worn by bullfighters and as a fashion item.

clue.text: Scan a photo possibly showing Native American woman

indicators.note: the letters could possibly be arranged another way

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Digitising an old photograph of a Native American woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder runs across three words, and the definition by example names the most famous Native American woman in popular memory.
explanation.definitionFit: Pocahontas was a Powhatan woman famous from early Virginia.

clue.text: Picked up routine flier

indicators.note: heard, as a radio picks up a signal

parts.note: a turn is a performer's routine

explanation.surface: Someone collects a regular leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' looks like a leaflet, but it is a bird; a turn is an act in a variety show.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this seabird is one of many things that fly, and 'flier' hides behind its leaflet sense.

clue.text: Extraordinary mega-fast gains primarily escalated over industrialisation period

indicators.note: out of the ordinary, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: 'primarily' means in the first place, so each word gives only the letter in its first place

parts.note: first letters of Escalated Over

explanation.surface: Very rapid gains shot up during the Industrial Revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gains' joins the two parts: the anagram fodder gains E and O.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for the Industrial Revolution, when steam engines powered factories and railways.

clue.text: On high netting starts to rig tackle of vessel

definitions.note: an adjective describing a blood vessel

indicators.note: netting means catching in a net, so the high word encloses the two letters

parts.note: aerial means up in the air, on high

indicators.note: starts to picks the first letter of each of the words rig and tackle

parts.note: the first letter of each word is used

explanation.surface: A sailor high in the rigging nets the tackle of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'netting' puts RT, the first letters of 'rig' and 'tackle' ('starts to'), into AERIAL. 'Vessel' suggests a ship, but here it is a blood vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Arterial describes an artery, the kind of blood vessel that carries blood from the heart.

clue.text: Shrimpers on a lagoon somewhat cold

indicators.note: only some of the words, so the answer is a part of them

parts.note: shrIMPERS ON A Lagoon

explanation.surface: People catching shrimp on a lagoon feel a bit chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold' looks like the weather on the lagoon; it is the emotional sense, a manner lacking warmth.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the emotional sense: a manner with no personal warmth is cold.

clue.text: Mechanics stripped fasteners beneath sump

indicators.note: beneath means below, so in this down entry the stripped word sits under the sump

parts.note: a sump is a pit where liquid collects

indicators.note: stripped means with the outer layer taken off, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: screws are fasteners

explanation.surface: Mechanics work under a car with fasteners stripped from the oil sump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sump' reads as the oil sump of an engine but means a pit. 'stripped' takes the ends off SCREWS (fasteners) to leave CREW, which goes 'beneath' PIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit crew is the team of mechanics who service a racing car during a race.

clue.text: Layer bearing wide cut

indicators.note: carrying, so holding the other part inside

parts.note: a hen is an egg layer
W is wide in cricket

explanation.surface: A layer containing a broad cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Layer' is not a stratum but something that lays: a hen. In cricket a wide is a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach.
explanation.definitionFit: Hewn means cut, as timber or stone is.

clue.text: Plain papers kept in case

indicators.note: placed inside the other part

parts.note: in case of an event
identity papers

explanation.surface: Ordinary documents stored in a folder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' reads as ordinary paper; it means obvious. 'Case' here is an occurrence, an event, not a box.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'plain' in the sense of clear or obvious, as in 'it was plain to everyone'.

clue.text: Sign that insect's entered outhouse

indicators.note: has gone into the other part

parts.note: Leo is a sign of the zodiac
an ant is an insect; the 's is 'has'

explanation.surface: A notice warns that an insect has got into the shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' looks like a notice on the shed door; it is a star sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a shed built against a wall, an outhouse.

clue.text: Assemble gun beside that woman

indicators.note: the parts sit next to each other

parts.note: gat is old slang for a gun
that woman is her

explanation.surface: Putting a gun together next to a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assemble' reads as putting the gun together in the surface; as the definition it means to bring together or collect.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to bring things or people together in one place.

clue.text: Rustic wooden frame is found in middle of wheelhouse

parts.note: a yoke is a wooden frame fitted over the necks of oxen

indicators.note: found in means sitting inside, so is goes within the middle letters
middle of picks out the central letters of wheelhouse

parts.note: its middle two letters are used

explanation.surface: A wooden frame is found in the middle of a boat's wheelhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: WHEELHOUSE has ten letters, so its middle is the pair at positions five and six, not one letter; the 'is' of the clue is used as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Yokelish means like a yokel, an unsophisticated country person, so it describes something rustic.

clue.text: Man is one heard somewhere in supermarket

indicators.note: what you hear, not what is written

parts.note: an aisle is a walkway between the shelves

explanation.surface: A man is heard somewhere in the supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Man, in the Irish Sea, is one of the British Isles.

clue.text: Concocted porky pies after losing both leads for dogs

indicators.note: made up, so the letters are rearranged
each word loses its first letter

parts.words: porky pies after losing both leads
parts.note: PORKY and PIES each lose their P

explanation.surface: Made-up porky pies with the dogs' leads gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Porky pies is rhyming slang for lies, so 'concocted porky pies' is a neat fit. Leads here are first letters, not dog leashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkies are Yorkshire terriers, small dogs.

clue.text: Maybe future ahead makes us become anxious

parts.note: the future is one grammatical tense
a team that is ahead is up

explanation.surface: Thinking about what lies ahead makes us worried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe future' is an example: the future is one grammatical tense.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: when nerves take hold the body stiffens, so becoming anxious is described this way.

clue.text: Novelist's wife makes changes to yarn — not on!

parts.note: W is wife
to change is to alter
COTTON without ON

explanation.surface: A novelist's wife keeps changing his story, and he objects.
explanation.walkthrough: The ‘s is 'is' joining definition to wordplay. 'Yarn' suggests a story, but it is cotton thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott was the Scottish novelist who wrote Ivanhoe.
